analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The Assault Weapons Ban of 2018 never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, with exemptions for law enforcement and certain other users. People who already owned these weapons could keep them, but would have to store them securely, and private sales of grandfathered weapons would require a licensed-dealer background check. It would also let states use existing federal anti-crime grant money to buy back the banned weapons and magazines.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities exposed to mass shootings and gun violence would benefit if the weapons covered by the bill — semiautomatic rifles like AR-15 and AK-types, certain pistols and shotguns, and magazines over 10 rounds — could no longer be newly manufactured or sold to civilians. The public would also gain a new record of which banned weapons are used in crimes, and residents of states that opt in could turn in banned weapons for compensation through buy-back programs.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices (over 10 rounds), with exemptions for law enforcement, retired officers, nuclear-materials security, antiques, and manually operated firearms.

Lets people keep weapons they already own, but requires secure storage out of the reach of people prohibited from having guns, and requires a licensed-dealer background check before a private sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon.
Allows state and local governments to use Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to compensate people who surrender banned weapons or magazines under buy-back programs.
Requires serial numbers and manufacture dates on newly made weapons and magazines, and directs the Attorney General to keep and publish a public record of banned weapons used in crimes.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms and magazine manufacturers and dealers would bear the main cost: they would lose the civilian market for the covered rifles, pistols, shotguns, and large-capacity magazines. Current owners of grandfathered weapons would face new storage obligations and dealer background checks on private sales, and buyers would no longer be able to purchase the covered firearms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun and magazine makers, dealers, owners

drawbacks.text: Weapons and magazines people already own stay in circulation under the bill's grandfather clause, so the ban would only affect future sales and would not remove existing weapons from communities.

The definitions sweep broadly: the ban covers any semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine plus a single common feature such as a pistol grip, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud, along with hundreds of named models, which would prohibit firearms many owners use for hunting, sport, and self-defense.

Buy-backs are voluntary: states and localities could use federal grant money to compensate people who surrender banned weapons, but no jurisdiction is required to run a program and no owner is required to participate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential public benefit is a smaller civilian supply of the semiautomatic weapons and high-capacity magazines most often associated with mass shootings, at a cost concentrated on manufacturers, dealers, and owners of the covered firearms. The bill's design limits its reach: grandfathered weapons stay in private hands indefinitely, the feature-based definitions would also prohibit many ordinary sporting firearms, and enforcement would fall to federal prosecutors and licensed dealers. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill's effect on existing violence would be gradual at best, while its restrictions on lawful owners and an entire retail category would be immediate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and died there without a hearing or a vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson introduced the bill on February 20, 2018, with Rep. David Cicilline as its only cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On March 20, 2018, it was referred to the subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, where no further action was taken.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing record, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and current owners came out ahead: with the bill never reaching a vote, the civilian market for semiautomatic rifles, pistols, shotguns, and large-capacity magazines remained unrestricted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers kept the market unchanged

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill, leaving it at the subcommittee level for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never brought an assault weapons ban to the House floor during the 115th Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association

sides.party_line_note: Both named sponsors and its single cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill never received a vote, so no roll-call exists; no Republican supported it on the record.

industries.note: The bill bans new manufacture and sale of AR-15 and AK-type rifles and hundreds of other named semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns, closing a major civilian market segment. The industry's interest in continuing those sales runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.
Manufacture and sale of any magazine, drum, or feeding device over 10 rounds would become a federal crime, eliminating a large product line.
Dealers could no longer sell covered weapons, and every private sale of a grandfathered weapon would have to run through a licensed dealer's background check, cutting into sales volume.
Current owners could keep grandfathered weapons but would face secure-storage requirements and dealer background checks on transfers, while would-be buyers lose access to the covered models.
